title: Origins of Cambodia: Preah Thong & Neang Neak
topic: Khmer founding legend · vocabulary of marriage, sea and royalty
note: Short myth retelling. Pause after each verse to check vocabulary and grammar, then ask the AI anything about the line.

verses.text: Long ago a foreign prince sailed across the sea to a new land.

questions.prompt: What does 'sailed across the sea' mean?
questions.answer: 'Sailed across the sea' means he travelled by boat over the ocean to get somewhere.

questions.prompt: Why is 'Long ago' at the start of the sentence?
questions.answer: 'Long ago' is a time phrase that sets a fairy-tale past. English often puts time first: Long ago + subject + verb.

verses.text: He met a dragon princess who lived in the kingdom by the water.

questions.answer: A princess who is also a dragon (or from a dragon family) — a magical royal woman in the legend.

questions.prompt: What does the relative clause 'who lived in the kingdom by the water' do?
questions.answer: It describes the princess. 'Who' refers to her; the clause tells us where she lived.

verses.text: They married, and the princess cut off her dragon tail to walk on land.

questions.prompt: What does the past tense pair 'married' and 'cut off' show?
questions.answer: Both verbs are simple past: completed actions in the story. English myths usually stay in the past throughout.
'Cut off' means she removed her tail — a dramatic change so she could live like a human on land.

verses.text: Their children became the first people of Cambodia.

questions.prompt: According to the legend, where do Cambodian people come from?
questions.answer: From the children of the foreign prince and the dragon princess — that is the founding story of the land.
'Became' is the past of 'become'. The legend is finished history, so English uses the past form.

verses.text: Even today, Khmer wedding customs remember the dragon princess.

questions.answer: The traditional things people do at a wedding — clothes, music, steps and symbols that families keep.
It contrasts the ancient legend with the present: the story still shapes modern weddings.

title: Sang Sinxay: The Epic Legend of Laos
topic: Lao epic · hero, journey, rescue vocabulary
note: Lao mythology retold in clear English. Pause on each verse for grammar and word study.

verses.text: Sang Sinxay was born with special powers and a brave heart.

questions.answer: It means he is courageous — not afraid to help others even when it is hard.
'Was born' is a fixed past-passive for birth. We say someone was born, not 'borned'.

verses.text: An ogre stole his aunt, so Sinxay set out on a long journey.

questions.prompt: What does 'set out on a journey' mean?
questions.answer: It means he started travelling with a clear purpose — here, to find his aunt.

questions.prompt: What does 'so' connect in this sentence?
questions.answer: 'So' shows result: the theft caused the journey. Cause first, result after 'so'.

verses.text: He fought many dangers and never gave up on his family.

questions.answer: He kept trying. 'Give up' means stop trying; 'never gave up' means he continued.
No — they are irregular. Fight → fought, give → gave. Learners must memorise them.

verses.text: At last he rescued his aunt and returned home as a hero.

questions.prompt: How does the epic end for Sinxay?
questions.answer: He saves his aunt and goes home celebrated as a hero — the classic rescue ending.
It signals the long wait is over: after many struggles, the success finally arrives.

verses.text: Lao people still tell this epic to teach courage and loyalty.

questions.answer: A long heroic story about a nation's legendary hero — bigger than a short fairy tale.
'To teach' shows purpose: they tell the story in order to teach courage and loyalty.

title: Learn English with Movies #1: The Incredibles
topic: Movie English · everyday phrases, stress and spoken grammar
note: Short ESL lesson built around a movie clip. Pause after each teaching beat, answer the grammar or vocabulary prompt, then ask the AI your own question.

verses.text: Watch the movie clip carefully — listen for how people really speak.

questions.answer: 'Listen for' means pay attention until you hear a specific word or sound, not just hear generally.

questions.prompt: Why is 'how people really speak' useful for learners?
questions.answer: Movie English is natural speech: reduced sounds, stress and everyday grammar you need beyond textbooks.

verses.text: Heroes hide their powers and try to live a normal family life.

questions.prompt: What does 'live a normal family life' mean?
questions.answer: It means everyday home routines — school, work, dinner — without superhero drama.

questions.prompt: Why are both verbs after 'and' in the present?
questions.answer: 'Hide' and 'try' are present simple for habits and ongoing situations in the story setup.

verses.text: Notice short spoken phrases like 'Come on!' and 'We've got to go.'

questions.answer: To urge someone to hurry, try harder, or follow — a friendly push, not a full sentence.

questions.prompt: What does "We've got to go" mean in formal English?
questions.answer: It means 'We have to go' / 'We must leave.' Spoken English prefers 'have got to' for urgency.

verses.text: Stress falls on the important words: GO, HELP, NOW — little words stay soft.

questions.answer: The beat you say louder and longer. Content words (go, help, now) carry stress; a/the/to stay soft.

questions.prompt: Why does English skip stress on 'little words'?
questions.answer: Articles and prepositions are grammar glue. Stressing content words helps listeners catch the message fast.

verses.text: Replay the clip and shadow the lines out loud to make the phrases yours.

questions.prompt: What does 'shadow' mean in language learning?
questions.answer: Speak along with the audio a split-second behind it — copy rhythm, stress and emotion.
First watch for meaning, then study the language, then speak it. Repetition turns phrases into usable English.
